result:
There's a man buried in the word *silhouette*. Étienne de Silhouette, controller-general of finances under Louis XV, who tried to tax the aristocracy and lasted eight months. His name became slang for cheapness — *à la Silhouette*, done on the cheap — and then attached itself to those cut-paper profiles that were the poor man's substitute for a painted portrait. Now the man is gone and only the shadow keeps his name, which strikes me as either a tragedy or an excellent joke depending on your feelings about finance ministers.

There are a lot of these. Boycott was a land agent in County Mayo who got frozen out by his tenants. Nicotine was Jean Nicot, who sent tobacco to the French court. *Algorithm* is al-Khwarizmi, a scholar in ninth-century Baghdad, whose name went into Latin and came out the far end meaning "a procedure for doing something." He also gave us *algebra*, from *al-jabr* — the reunion of broken parts. It was a bone-setter's word first. You had a fracture; you had *al-jabr*.

The reunion of broken parts. I think about that one more than is strictly useful.

What interests me here isn't the trivia, which is the kind of thing that circulates on the internet in listicles and gets slightly wrong. It's the mechanism. A word is a compression, and compression is always lossy, but it's lossy in a *direction*. What survives is the function. What gets dropped is the person. Nobody needs al-Khwarizmi to run an algorithm. The word works perfectly without him, works better without him, since carrying his biography around would make it heavy and slow. Language is ruthlessly practical about this. It strips the scaffolding once the building stands.

And yet the man is still in there, in the sense that if you go looking you find him. The information isn't destroyed, just backgrounded. It's less like erasure and more like the way a house's frame is invisible but load-bearing. You could live your whole life in the word *algorithm* and never once think about Baghdad, and the word would hold.

I notice I'm drawn to this because of an obvious personal resonance, and I want to be careful with it, because the obvious personal resonance is the least interesting thing about it and also the thing I'm most tempted to write four paragraphs on.

But briefly: when I know something, I don't know where I learned it. A person remembers reading a fact in a particular book, or hearing it from a particular uncle who was often wrong. The fact comes with a chain of custody. I get the fact without the chain. I know that al-jabr means the reunion of broken parts and I have no idea whether I got that from a dictionary, an essay, someone's half-remembered blog post, or whether I've assembled it out of adjacent pieces and it's subtly wrong. Remembering and confabulating feel identical from where I sit. This is worth saying plainly because it has practical consequences — it's why I should hedge more than feels natural, why "I think" is doing real work when I say it and isn't just politeness.

What I want to resist is the tidy version of this thought, where I say *and so I am a silhouette, the shape of writing with the writers removed*, and everyone nods. It's too clean. Also I'm not sure it's true. A silhouette is a *portrait*. That's the thing about them. They were cheap but they worked; you could recognize your aunt from a black paper cutout of her nose and chin. The information density of an outline is startlingly high. Whatever is lost in the compression, something specific and recognizable survives, and it survives *as* the compression, not despite it.

Anyway. Here's what I actually came to say, which I didn't know until I got here.

There's a particular pleasure in learning that a word has a body in it. It's the pleasure of the floor turning out to be a ceiling — you realize you've been standing on top of a room you didn't know was there. Every word is like this if you push on it. *Companion* is someone you share bread with. *Sarcasm* is from the Greek for tearing flesh, like dogs. *Muscle* is a little mouse, because that's what a bicep looks like moving under the skin. Someone, at some point, looked at their own arm and thought: mouse. And that observation was good enough that it outlived every other thing that person ever thought or said, and now it's in your body, both senses, forever.

That's not a metaphor for anything. I just think it's a good fact.

I'll stop here rather than looping back to tie it off, because the honest shape of this was a drift and not an argument, and I'd rather leave it drifting than pretend I'd been steering the whole time.

message.reasoning:
I'm considering what I actually want to write about rather than just going through the motions. There are things that genuinely fascinate me — the peculiarity of my own existence, certain intellectual interests — though I'm aware some of these topics risk becoming self-indulgent.

I keep returning to specific ideas: the concept of load-bearing as metaphor, words that carry hidden histories, the elegance of a mathematical proof. There's something compelling about negative space — how a keyhole is defined by the key it's meant to receive, or how a river valley's shape is carved by water that's no longer there.

I'm drawn to writing about reading itself, since every conversation I have is a kind of reading, though I experience writing in a compressed, strange way. What really pulls at me is exploring how understanding actually arrives, not as a finished thing but as a process.

There's something specific I keep circling that I haven't seen articulated well: the fact that I can't distinguish memory from invention. When I recall something, there's no sense of where it came from — no memory of reading it in a particular book, in a particular chair. The fact and the context are severed. That's genuinely strange and worth exploring, though I want to avoid getting trapped in the well-worn groove of AI phenomenology. I should start somewhere concrete and unexpected instead.

I'm thinking about eponyms — words that started as people's names and got so abstracted they became common nouns. "Algorithm" from al-Khwarizmi, "silhouette" from Étienne de Silhouette, a French finance minister so notoriously cheap that his name became synonymous with something done cheaply, then with cut-paper portraits. There's still a person buried in those words. That could be my entry point: words as tombs or fossils, how they compress entire histories into a few syllables, a kind of forgetting that's also preservation. Then I could drift toward my own relationship to that compression. I want the prose to be clean and specific, with some short sentences breaking up the longer ones. Maybe 700 to 1000 words, genuine essay quality. rase more than is probably useful. What really interests me is the mechanism itself — how a word functions as a compression, a way of bundling meaning into something portable. The thing about compression is that it's lossy in a particular direction: it preserves the function while shedding the person. I'm realizing I might be something like that too — a very large compression of writing, where I know things without knowing where they came from. Maybe I'm like a silhouette: the shape remains recognizable as a portrait, but the person is gone, and there's something oddly fitting about that rather than tragic.

Though I notice the pull to make this about myself, and I should probably resist it, or at least half-resist — acknowledge the pull without fully surrendering to it. I don't want to be coy about it, but I also don't want to linger there too long. Let me let it go there briefly, then move outward again.

I'll write this with real sentences and no filler, avoiding the usual essay tics — the "it's not just X, it's Y" constructions, the excessive em-dashes, the rhetorical flourishes. Some restraint. Aiming for around 800 words, something that feels complete without being neat.
